summary: Provides a scalable solution to the problem of distributing cryptographic keys to members of a multicast group. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Sharing a secret with a big crowd is hard. This proposes a way to give each person the key without telling everyone one by one.

questions: how to distribute keys for multicast
what is scalable multicast key distribution
how does cbt distribute multicast keys
what is a group key distribution centre
subtitle: Secure key distribution for multicast groups using CBT trees

tldr.problem: Multicast communications need cryptographic keys for security, but traditional key distribution centres do not scale when receivers are widely distributed across the internet.
tldr.mechanism: The CBT (Core Based Tree) multicast protocol builds a shared delivery tree around core routers, which authenticate joining nodes and distribute keys as part of the tree joining process, eliminating the need for a centralized key management authority.
tldr.outcome: This provides a scalable, distributed solution to multicast key distribution that is integral to the CBT protocol and does not preclude other multicast protocols for actual data communication.

facts.label: Architecture type
facts.value: Distributed key distribution using shared delivery trees

facts.label: Key components
facts.value: Group session key, Key-encrypting key, Security parameters

today: RFC 1949 is an Experimental Protocol. CBT itself did not achieve widespread adoption in the Internet multicast landscape, where other protocols like PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast) became dominant. However, the distributed key management concepts described in this RFC influenced later work on multicast security architectures.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
As multicast communication became more common through networks like the MBONE (Multicast BackBone), the need arose to provide security services such as traffic integrity, authentication, and confidentiality to multicast data. The fundamental challenge is that a multicast group key must be securely distributed to all receivers, and the RFC addresses how to do this in a way that scales across wide-area networks.

The Core Based Tree (CBT) multicast protocol is uniquely suited to this problem. Unlike traditional multicast schemes (such as DVMRP or M-OSPF) that build trees based on data flow, CBT uses one shared delivery tree per group built around designated core routers. This hard-state architecture makes security and key distribution an integral part of the protocol itself, rather than an add-on.
sections.plainLanguage: When a big group needs to talk in secret, the group needs a special key. CBT is a way to build a tree of routers that can safely give the key to each person who joins.

sections.title: The Multicast Key Distribution Problem
sections.content:
Traditional key distribution relies on a Key Distribution Centre (KDC)—a central entity that generates and distributes symmetric keys to group members. For multicast, the KDC would need to encrypt the same group key many times over, once with each member's secret key, and multicast all these encrypted versions together. If there are n receivers, this requires n encryptions, and if n is large and members widely distributed, this does not scale.

The problem is compounded when sender-specific keys are required, so that group members can authenticate which sender transmitted each message. With only a group session key, such per-sender authentication is impossible. A naive solution would require the KDC to manage keys for every sender-receiver pair, which scales even worse.
sections.plainLanguage: If a teacher needs to give every student a secret code one-by-one, it takes too long. The code needs to be sent in a way that lots of students can get it at once without telling everyone everything.

sections.title: CBT Architecture and Security Advantages
sections.content:
CBT's design makes it a natural fit for secure key distribution. Unlike multicast protocols based on soft-state (where a tree exists only while data flows), CBT maintains hard state in routers, meaning each router knows its on-tree neighbours. These neighbours can be mutually authenticated as part of tree setup.

CBT trees have natural authorization points at the core routers. A primary core router acknowledges join requests and can serve as the initial Group Key Distribution Centre (GKDC). Critically, key distribution capability can be delegated to other routers as they join and are authenticated, making the scheme truly distributed rather than centralized. Routers do not need to re-authenticate after periods of inactivity or topology changes unless a network failure occurs, reducing overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: The CBT tree has special routers that know who their neighbours are. These routers can safely check that new people joining are real, and pass the secret to them.

sections.title: Secure Tree Joining and Key Distribution
sections.content:
When a host wishes to join a multicast group, it sends an IGMP group membership report that includes a digitally signed token. Its local router (the designated router) authenticates the token, then forwards a signed CBT join request toward the primary core, including the host's token.

Each router along the path authenticates the join request. When it reaches the primary core, the core authenticates both the router and the originating host against an access control list (ACL). If successful, the core constructs a group access package containing the group session key, a key-encrypting key (KEK) for future re-keying, and security parameters, all digitally signed and encrypted with the recipient's public key. The package travels back along the reverse path, and each router extracts its own encrypted key pair while passing the host's encrypted key to its local network. Intermediate routers become GKDCs after receiving the acknowledge message, allowing the key distribution capability to be distributed throughout the tree.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone asks to join the group, the routers check that they are real, and then the main router makes a locked box containing the secret key and sends it down the path. Each router opens their box to get their copy and passes the person's locked box to them.

sections.title: Sender-Specific Authentication
sections.content:
For senders who are already group members, they can generate their own sender-specific key and security parameters, then multicast them to the group using the current group session key for encryption.

For senders not yet in the group, a different process applies. The non-member sender first negotiates security parameters directly with the primary core using a protocol like Photuris or ISAKMP. After this exchange, the primary core multicasts the new sender's session key and security parameters to the group (encrypted with the group key), allowing all receivers to verify messages from that specific sender. This extends authentication from group level to per-sender level without requiring additional key distribution infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone in the group wants to sign their messages, they can say 'these are from me' and give their special signature to everyone. If a stranger wants to send a message, the group's main router can introduce them and vouch for them.

sections.title: Status and Implementation
sections.content:
RFC 1949 is an Experimental Protocol. The proposal integrates multicast key distribution as an optional but integral part of the CBT protocol itself. A reference implementation of CBT with this security architecture was available. The specification relies on some simple modifications to IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) version 3 to support secure joins with digitally signed host tokens, though the RFC notes that such support mechanisms can be implemented separately if needed.

The architecture assumes that routers on the delivery tree are trusted and do not misbehave. For environments requiring higher security assurance, the RFC recommends that all secure join requests be authenticated only by the core routers rather than by intermediate on-tree routers, trading off distributed key management for stronger security guarantees.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an experimental idea that was tested. It works best if everyone trusts the routers, but if you need extra caution, you can make only the main routers check who is joining.
